summary: Children aged 8–9 learn to distinguish conductors (materials that let electricity flow) from insulators (materials that block it), and to generalise that most metals are good conductors while most non-metals are insulators. The core method is empirical: place a material in the gap of a simple circuit and see whether the bulb lights. The curriculum frames this as a hands-on enquiry; the primary activity is a predict–test–record investigation with a real materials kit, with on-screen or interactive-image work as useful companions for prediction, varied material sets, instant recording, and fixing vocabulary.
misconceptions: 'All metals are magnetic / all shiny things conduct' — conflating conduction with magnetism or shininess; the test, not appearance, decides (a shiny painted surface may not conduct).
Thinking the plastic-coated wire conducts along its plastic, or not realising the metal inside is the conductor and the plastic the insulator.
Believing an insulator in the gap 'slows' the electricity rather than stopping the loop entirely — at this level it simply doesn't light.
Overgeneralising from one metal or assuming non-metals never conduct (graphite/pencil lead is a useful counter-case).
Thinking thickness or size of the object determines conduction rather than the material it is made of.

activities.title: Predict–test–record with a gapped circuit
steps: Set up (or use) a test circuit with a battery, bulb and a gap bridged by two crocodile clips, so the circuit itself is the test instrument.
For each material, first write a prediction: 'Will the bulb light? Conductor or insulator?' before testing.
Drop or clip the material across the gap, observe whether the bulb lights, and log the result in a table with columns: material | prediction | result (conductor/insulator).
Test a deliberately wide, varied set: several metals (steel paperclip, copper strip, aluminium, a coin), plus wood (lolly stick), plastic (ruler), rubber band, glass, paper, and fabric.
After testing, step back and look at the filled table: notice that the conductor column has filled with metals while wood, plastic, rubber and glass sit in the insulator column.
State the pattern you discovered in your own words, e.g. 'metals are the good conductors'.
activities.insight: Whether a material conducts is decided by what it is made of, not how it looks. Testing a varied set lets the 'metals are good conductors' generalisation emerge from the child's own evidence rather than being asserted.

activities.title: Surprise cards: testing the rule's edges
steps: Predict and then test a dull or unpolished metal object (making sure the clip touches bare metal, not a tarnished patch) against a shiny object that does not conduct at its surface — for example a shiny plastic object (a non-metal), or a painted metal tab where the clips touch only the paint, which insulates so the bulb stays dark even though the tab is metal underneath — saying which you think will light the bulb AND why before testing.

Test a pencil-lead / graphite rod as a 'huh?' case: graphite is a non-metal that conducts. A thin pencil lead also contains clay and is a poorer conductor than metal, so a filament bulb may glow only dimly or not visibly. A short, thick graphite rod, or an LED or buzzer in place of the bulb, shows the effect more reliably.
Compare hard glass and hard wood (both insulators) with a softer metal, to check whether hardness decides conduction.
Discuss as enrichment: graphite conducts, and pure water barely conducts — these are interesting exceptions, not the core rule.
activities.insight: Surface cues like shininess and hardness do not decide conduction: a dull metal still conducts (where the clip reaches bare metal), while a shiny plastic or a painted-over metal still blocks current at its surface. 'Most metals conduct' and 'most non-metals insulate' is the calibrated claim, with a few noted exceptions.

activities.title: Why wires are made the way they are
steps: Examine (or view a cutaway of) an electrical wire: identify the metal core and the plastic sheath.
Explain which part conducts (the metal core) and which part insulates and keeps us safe (the plastic coating).
Connect to the loop rule: an insulator placed in the gap is just another kind of break, so the bulb simply does not light.
activities.insight: A wire deliberately combines a conductor (metal core to carry the electricity) and an insulator (plastic sheath to keep the electricity contained and us safe). An insulator in the circuit gap stops the loop rather than slowing the electricity.

activities.title: Sort and check (classification practice)
steps: Sort a set of materials into two groups: conductors and insulators, with metals highlighted as a cue.
Answer 'which of these would make the bulb light?' selection questions and match materials to their category.
For any unfamiliar material, describe how you would turn it into a fair test for conduction (place it in the circuit gap, keep the rest of the circuit the same, see if the bulb lights).
activities.insight: Consolidate and check the conductor/insulator vocabulary and the metals generalisation, and recognise that a fair circuit test — not appearance — settles uncertain cases.

checkQuestion: You test a shiny plastic ruler and a dull piece of iron in a circuit. The shiny ruler doesn't let the bulb light, but the dull iron does. Your friend expected the shiny one to conduct because 'shiny things carry electricity.' What actually decides whether a material conducts?
checkAnswer: What decides it is what the material is made of, not how it looks: metals conduct electricity (let current flow through), while most non-metals such as plastic, wood and rubber are insulators (block it). Shininess doesn't decide it — a shiny plastic still blocks current and a dull metal still conducts. The iron conducts because it's a metal; the ruler blocks it because it's plastic.
